sections.on_device_hybrid:
Running the classifier fully on the phone is the right shape for the everyday case but not for the hard cases. The surviving design is hybrid: fine-tune a small, distilled version of the classifier to run on-device; when its top confidence falls below a fixed threshold (e.g., 0.6), the app uploads the photo for the original full-size server model to take a second pass. This answers the open question of what to do when the model is unsure — escalate rather than guess — and keeps the original accuracy claim for exactly the cases where the gardener needs the better model, while preserving offline use and photo privacy for the routine ones. Escalation also gives a natural pipeline for collecting the real-garden hard examples that are otherwise missing from the training data.

Unverified: the threshold value, and whether the on-device model's confidences are calibrated well enough for escalation to fire at the right times.

nodes.text:
# Leaf-photo plant disease check for home gardeners
_Let a gardener photograph a sick leaf with their phone and get told which disease it probably is._

## the problem it addresses
Home gardeners cannot tell plant diseases apart, so they either do nothing or spray the wrong treatment.

## description
A phone app where the gardener photographs a leaf that looks wrong. An image classifier trained on labelled photographs of diseased leaves returns the three most likely diseases with a confidence for each, plus a short description of what to do about the top one. The claim is that most common garden diseases are visually distinctive enough that a phone photo is sufficient, so no lab test or expert is needed for the everyday cases.

## addresses gaps
gap_demo01

## technique
Fine-tune an off-the-shelf image classifier on a public dataset of labelled diseased-leaf photographs. The app sends the photo to a server, the server returns the top three labels with confidences. Show the top three, not just the best guess, so the gardener can tell when the model is unsure.

## open_questions
- Do photos taken in a real garden work as well as the clean dataset photos taken against a plain background?
- How should the app behave when the model is unsure about all three guesses?
nodes.title: Leaf-photo plant disease check for home gardeners

nodes.text: The app ships a fine-tuned mobile-class model (e.g., MobileNetV3-Large or EfficientNet-Lite) quantized to a few MB and does all inference locally. This makes the app work offline, keeps garden photos on the phone, and removes per-photo server cost, at the price of accepting a lower accuracy ceiling than the original full-size model. The real-garden/plain-background gap question becomes more pressing, not less: a smaller model is less robust to background clutter, so the training mix must include real-garden photos before launch.
nodes.title: Run entirely on the phone: replace the server with a compact quantized model and keep the top-three-with-confidences behaviour unchanged.
nodes.comparison: Loses because it restates the plan on a smaller model and concedes the real-garden gap is more pressing without proposing any answer to the unsure-behaviour open question.
nodes.question: Is there a published accuracy figure for a quantized mobile-class model fine-tuned on the chosen public plant-disease dataset on real-garden photos rather than clean dataset photos?

nodes.text: The on-device model handles the everyday case, but when its top confidence falls below a fixed threshold (e.g., 0.6), the app uploads the photo for the original full-size server model to take a second pass. This is a concrete answer to the open question 'how should the app behave when unsure?', and it keeps the original claim's accuracy for exactly the cases where a gardener needs the better model, while preserving offline use and privacy for the routine ones. Escalation also gives a natural pipeline for collecting the real-garden hard examples that are otherwise missing from the training data.
nodes.title: Hybrid: run the small model on the phone and escalate to the server model only when the top three confidences are all low.

outcome.answer: It works, but not as an either/or — the design that survives is a hybrid: a small, distilled classifier runs on the phone for the everyday case, and when its top confidence falls below a fixed threshold (e.g., 0.6) the photo is uploaded for the original full-size server model to take a second pass. That keeps offline use and photo privacy for routine cases while preserving the original accuracy claim exactly where the gardener needs the better model, and the escalations double as a collection pipeline for the real-garden hard examples the training set lacks. The 'unsure' open question gets a concrete answer — escalate rather than guess. What still needs verification is the threshold value and whether the on-device model's confidences are calibrated well enough to make escalation fire at the right times.
proposed_changes: technique: Describe the hybrid architecture instead of 'the app sends the photo to a server': a small on-device classifier handles the everyday case, and upload happens only when its top confidence falls below a threshold (e.g., 0.6), triggering the full server model as a second pass.
